readings.title: Checking a photograph before sharing
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A neighbourhood group received a dramatic photograph said to show a recent local flood. Several members recognised an older building in the background. The main obstacle was an image without a reliable date. The message named no photographer or exact location, yet it spread quickly through chat groups. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a search for the original image source. Members compared visible landmarks and found an archived version from a different year. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated the photograph was old and misleadingly described. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a correction linked to the dated original. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: a convincing image still needs context. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in checking a photograph before sharing, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Reading a survey headline
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A news page claimed that almost everyone wanted a new park rule. The linked survey had been answered by only a small group. The main obstacle was a headline that overstated limited responses. Most respondents belonged to one club and had been invited through its own mailing list. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a look at sample size and recruitment. Students read the method notes and compared the headline with the actual survey question. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated the result could not represent all residents. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a summary that reports who answered. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: numbers require an explanation of their source. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in reading a survey headline, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Finding the source of health advice
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A popular post offered simple health advice but named no author. Readers in a class asked whether its claims came from qualified sources. The main obstacle was advice without an identifiable expert. The post used confident language and attractive images in place of references. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a check against official health information. The tutor compared the claims with current material from a recognised health service. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated several claims lacked supporting evidence. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a source checklist and a link to qualified guidance. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: important claims deserve traceable evidence. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in finding the source of health advice, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A headline about a school change
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Parents saw an online headline saying a school had cancelled its music classes. The article described only a temporary room move. The main obstacle was a title that distorted the full announcement. Some readers shared the headline without opening the detailed notice. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a comparison with the school statement. Parents checked the published timetable and asked staff which lessons were affected. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated classes were continuing in another room. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a short correction that quotes the timetable. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: reading beyond a headline prevents confusion. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a headline about a school change, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for media and information literacy must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the community media learning programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 关于媒介与信息素养的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the information literacy team about a community activity related to media and information literacy. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the community media learning programme. People have noticed an image without a reliable date, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
